newsitem.title: USA: AMR agrees to buy Boeing jets in $6 billion deal.
newsitem.headline: AMR agrees to buy Boeing jets in $6 billion deal.

text.p: American Airlines has agreed to buy more than $6 billion worth of Boeing Co. jetliners in a major victory for the world's biggest airplane manufacturer, a source at the airline said Wednesday.
The source, who asked not to be identified, said directors of the airline's parent, AMR Corp. agreed to buy more than 100 Boeing jets worth "close to $6.5 billion" based on list prices.
The nation's second-largest airline agreed to buy about 75 Boeing 737 jets, 12 each of the manufacturer's 777s and 757s, and three or four Boeing 767s, he said.
The source said he understood the carrier also will acquire options on additional jets valued at over $20 billion, making the order one of the biggest commercial jetliner orders ever.
Officials of Boeing and American declined to comment, but AMR Chairman Robert Crandall was scheduled to make a "major company announcement" at a news conference Thursday.
Although American officials have said privately they have chosen Boeing for their fleet modernization program, the exact size of the initial order had not been revealed.

The orders were expected to be contingent on ratification by pilots of a new six-year contract, which will go before 9,150 union members next month. The union board voted 10-8 Wednesday to approve the tentative pact reached in September.

"I think basically this is a commitment to the Boeing family," analyst Bill Whitlow of Pacific Crest Securities said, noting that American currently operates a a mix of planes built by Boeing, McDonnell Douglas Corp., Airbus Industrie and Fokker NV.

"If you look at their fleet, they (American) have kind of a hodgepodge of things," he said. "I think you can make the case that most of the airplanes they will be buying in the future will be these Boeing models."

American's decision would be yet another blow for McDonnell Douglas, which has acknowledged it will be only a niche player in the commercial aircraft market. Last week it was knocked out of contention for a new fighter plane, the Pentagon's biggest weapons program of the early 21st century.

American is the largest operator of McDonnell Douglas' narrowbody MD-80 jets, with some 260 airplanes, but relations between the two companies soured when the larger MD-11 model failed to meet initial performance standards, analysts said.

American has announced plans to sell most of its MD-11s to Federal Express Corp. for use as cargo jets, and analysts said Boeing's 777 would be a likely replacement, suitable for American's potential expansion in the Far East.

"Ordering the new-generation 737 is a major policy shift for American," said Scott Hamilton, editor of Commercial Aviation Report. "It is a huge win for Boeing, and it is a tremendous blow to Douglas and its MD-90/95 family."

American currently does not operate the 737, the world's most popular jetliner, which seats from 108 to 189 passengers and initially will be used to replace the 75 older 727 jets used by the airline. The airline also reportedly will order Boeing 757s and 767s.
Analyst Paul Nisbet of JSA Research said American appears to be turning over "the whole fleet to Boeing aircraft."
Analysts said they still expected a big fleet-renewal order from No. 3 carrier Delta Air Lines Inc., which could go at least partly to McDonnell Douglas.
"Somewhere along the line this is going to bubble over in McDonell Douglas' favor," Nisbet said.
Boeing stock rose $2.375 to $96.375 and AMR stock lost 62.5 cents to $91, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
